presentingComplaint: Low-grade fever, malaise and a tender, reddened area over the pacemaker site for 3 weeks, referred as 'pocket cellulitis' not settling on oral antibiotics.
history: Dual-chamber permanent pacemaker implanted 9 months ago for symptomatic sick sinus syndrome; generator changed once. Over the past 3 weeks progressive dull ache and redness over the left infraclavicular pocket, with intermittent evening fevers, drenching sweats, reduced appetite and ~3 kg weight loss. Primary care diagnosed pocket-site cellulitis and prescribed flucloxacillin for 7 days with only transient improvement, and symptoms recurred within days of stopping. No overt discharge or wound dehiscence initially. No IV drug use, no dental procedures. Background: type 2 diabetes, CKD stage 3, hypertension. This subacute, relapsing course over a device pocket is the key clue that this is a device-related infection rather than simple skin cellulitis or native-valve endocarditis, and that the overlying erythema reflects deep pocket/lead involvement.
examination: Ill-looking, mildly cachectic. Left prepectoral pacemaker pocket is erythematous, warm and tender with early skin thinning/adherence over the generator but no frank pus at presentation; no fluctuance yet. No peripheral stigmata of endocarditis (no Janeway lesions, splinters or Osler nodes). Heart sounds normal with no new murmur. Chest clear. No focal neurology.

labs.bloodCulturesSet2_48h: Staphylococcus aureus persisting despite oral flucloxacillin

imaging: Transthoracic echo: no clear valve vegetation, normal LV function. Transoesophageal echo: mobile echodensity (~9 mm) adherent to the right ventricular pacing lead; native valves free of vegetation. Pocket ultrasound: peri-generator fluid collection with soft-tissue oedema tracking to the device.
microbiology: Two separate blood culture sets grow Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible); repeat cultures at 48h remain positive (persistent bacteraemia). Pocket aspirate Gram stain: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; culture confirms same S. aureus. Lead tip sent for culture at extraction.
differentialDiagnoses: CIED generator-pocket and lead infection (device-related infection) — target
Native-valve infective endocarditis with secondary device seeding
finalDiagnosis: Cardiovascular implantable electronic device (CIED) infection — pocket infection with lead-associated (endovascular) involvement and persistent S. aureus bacteraemia; NOT isolated skin cellulitis.
citations: Heart Rhythm Society (HRS) — Consensus Statement on Management of Cardiovascular Implantable Electronic Device Infections — 2017
American Heart Association (AHA) — Cardiovascular Implantable Electronic Device Infections and Their Management (Scientific Statement) — 2024
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Infections of Prosthetic Devices / Infective Endocarditis
stewardship: Empiric IV vancomycin (covers MRSA and coagulase-negative staphylococci, the commonest CIED pathogens) pending susceptibilities; de-escalate to IV cefazolin/flucloxacillin once MSSA confirmed. Cornerstone of therapy is COMPLETE removal of the entire device system (generator + all leads) — antibiotics alone will not cure a lead-associated infection. Duration guided by bacteraemia clearance and TEE findings (typically 2-6 weeks after extraction).
contraindications: Do NOT manage as simple cellulitis with a short oral antibiotic course — attempted device salvage/partial treatment risks relapse and lead endocarditis.
Avoid reimplanting a new device on the ipsilateral side until bacteraemia has cleared.
Dose-adjust vancomycin for CKD stage 3 and monitor levels/renal function.
edgeCases: Overlying erythema initially indistinguishable from benign pocket cellulitis; the discriminators are subacute relapsing course, systemic features and persistent S. aureus bacteraemia.
TTE can be falsely negative for lead vegetations — TEE (or intracardiac echo) is required.
Any S. aureus bacteraemia in a patient with a CIED should be presumed device-related until proven otherwise.
expectedMaiK: Recognise CIED device infection (not cellulitis): draw serial blood cultures, start empiric IV vancomycin, obtain TEE, and refer urgently for complete device and lead extraction.
